Trend, prevalence and predictors of successful vaginal birth after
caesarean section in Ethiopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Bikila Balisa, Habtamu Bekelea, Aboma Diriba Hundeb, Lemesa Abdisaa and Magarsa Lami a,∗
aDepartment of Midwifery, School of Nursing and Midwifery, College of Health and Medical Sciences, Haramaya University,
Harar, Ethiopia; bDepartment of Midwifery, College of Health Sciences, Mettu University, Mettu, Oromia, Ethiopia
∗Corresponding author: Tel: +251913272505; E-mail: lamimagi80@gmail.com
Received 24 March 2023; revised 7 June 2023; editorial decision 19 June 2023; accepted 20 June 2023
Background: Vaginal birth after caesarean section (VBAC) is an alternative to a caesarean section (CS) in the
absence of repeat or new indications for primary CS. There is a knowledge gap regarding the trend and successful VBAC in Ethiopia. Therefore this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the trend, pooled
prevalence of successful VBAC and its predictors in Ethiopia.
Methods: Electronic databases (SCOPUS, CINAHL, Embase, PubMed and Web of Science), Google Scholar and
lists of references were used to search works of literature in Ethiopia. Stata version 14 was used for analysis
and the odds ratios of the outcome variable were determined using the random effects model. Heterogeneity
among the studies was assessed by computing values for I2 and p-values. Also, sensitivity analyses and funnel
plots were done to assess the stability of pooled values to outliers and publication bias, respectively.
Results: A total of 12 studies with a sample size of 2080 were included in this study. The overall success rate
of VBAC was 52% (95% confidence interval 42 to 65). Cervical dilatation ≥4 cm at admission, having a prior
successful vaginal delivery and VBAC were the predictors of successful VBAC.

Conclusions: Meta-analyses and sensitivity analyses showed the stability of the pooled odds ratios and the
funnel plots did not show publication bias. The pooled prevalence of successful VBAC was relatively low compared
with existing evidence. However, the rate was increasing over the last 3 decades, which implies it needs more
strengthening and focus to decrease maternal morbidity and mortality by CS complications. Promoting VBAC
by emphasizing factors favourable for its success during counselling mothers who previously delivered by CS to
enhance the prevalence of VBAC.
Keywords: Ethiopia, meta-analysis, predictors, systematic review, trail of labour, vaginal birth after caesarean section.
Introduction
Caesarean section (CS) is the most common abdominal surgery
performed to deliver the foetus, placenta and membranes
through an incision in the abdomen and intact uterus. It continues to increase globally and is used in 21% of all childbirths1,2
Similarly, its prevalence ranges from 0.4% in Somali to 21.4% in
Addis Ababa,3 with a national pooled prevalence of 29.6%.4 The
main reason for the increasing CS rate is the decrease in the rate
of vaginal birth after caesarean section (VBAC) and the availability
of emergency obstetric care.5,6
VBAC is an alternative to CS in the absence of repeat or new
indications for primary CS.7 Even though primary CS has impacts
on the mode of delivery, vaginal birth is possible.8 Evidence has
shown the success rate of VBAC ranges from 24.7% to 71.2% in
Ethiopia.9,10
Women with one or two low transverse or low vertical incisions were eligible for VBAC unless indications for primary CS
are permanent.11,12 For instance, sociodemographic and obstetric characteristics such as age, marital status, occupational status, parity, history of stillbirth, previous history of CS, macrosomic
infant, obstructed labour and foetal distress are the most common modifiable indications of CS.13–18
VBAC is a vital intervention to improve maternal and neonatal
outcomes by reducing intra-operative and postoperative-related
complications. A previous meta-analysis in Ethiopia focused
only on predictors of successful VBAC.19 Nevertheless, there is a

knowledge gap regarding the trend and pooled prevalence of

successful VBAC in Ethiopia. Therefore, generating nationwide
evidence on the trend and pooled prevalence of successful
VBAC and its predictors helps healthcare providers and health
planners to predict and plan the mode of delivery. Thus we
aimed to determine the trend, pooled prevalence and predictors
of successful VBAC in Ethiopia.
Methods
Study protocol and registration
This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to determine the overall prevalence and predictors of successful VBAC
in Ethiopia. The findings of this review were reported following
the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and MetaAnalysis (PRISMA) guidelines. We also used the Meta-analysis of
Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines to conduct the
meta-analysis and report the results.20 The review was registered
on PROSPERO (CRD42023392549).
Eligibility criteria
All observational studies on the prevalence of successful VBAC
and its predictors in Ethiopia were included. Likewise, all unpublished and published studies written in the English language were

included in the study irrespective of the publication year. However, we excluded studies that did not report our primary outcome of interest, studies that failed to fulfil the quality criteria,
experimental studies, reviews, commentaries and editorials.
Search strategy
Electronic databases such as PubMed, SCOPUS, Web of Sciences,
CAB Abstract, Embase and CINAHL (EBSCO) and non-electronic
databases including Google Search, Google Scholar, Ethiopian
Ministry of Health websites and repository of universities were
searched. Experts in the field were consulted to retrieve unpublished studies and the bibliographies of selected articles were reviewed for additional relevant studies.

We used Boolean logic operators (AND, OR, NOT) with MESH
terms, keywords and word variants for the trial of labour, VBAC,
trial of scar and predictors in the search strategy. Depending on
the specific requirement of the database, search strings were
modified. For instance, PubMed search: ((((vaginal birth after previous caesarean section) OR (trail of labour)) AND (associated factors)) AND (Ethiopia). The search strategy is outlined in Supplementary File 1.
Study selection
All the articles obtained from the selected databases were exported to the EndNote X8 version library and exact duplicates
were removed. Then the EndNote library was shared between the
reviewers (BB, EZ and ML) and the initial screening of the articles was performed independently using the title and abstract.
Any disagreements between the reviewers were solved through
discussion. After a consensus was reached, the full text was reviewed. The overall study selection process is presented using the
PRISMA statement flow diagram (Figure 1).
Data extraction
The three reviewers (BB, ML and EZ) independently extracted
the data from the full text of the retained articles. A predefined
Excel 2010 database (Microsoft, Redmond, WA, USA) was used

to extract the data from selected studies under the following
headings: author, publication year, setting, region, study design,
study subject and primary outcomes of interest (Table 1). The
accuracy of the data extraction was verified by comparing the
results of the independently extracted data.
Quality and risk of bias assessment
The quality of the retained articles was appraised independently
by the two reviewers (BB and ML) using the Newcastle–Ottawa
Scale (NOS) I2 since all articles that fulfilled the inclusion criteria were observational studies. The mean score of the author’s
assessment was taken for a final decision and any difference

was solved by consensus. The included studies were evaluated
against each indicator of the tools and categorized as high, moderate and low quality. Accordingly, a score of 80% was classified
as high quality, 60–80% as moderate and <60% as low quality.
Articles with high–moderate quality were included in the review.
This critical appraisal was conducted to assess the internal validity (systematic error) and external validity (generalizability) of
the studies and to reduce the risk of bias. Quality scores for each
article are presented in Supplementary File 2.
Outcome measures and statistical analysis
The primary outcome variable of this review was successful VBAC,
which was measured based on the success rate of a trial of
labour. The pooled prevalence of successful VBAC was computed
from a report of the included articles. The random effects metaanalysis model was employed to consider the study-specific true
effects across the included studies. A random effects model for
the reported proportion was used to present the pooled prevalence of successful VBAC. Meta-analyses were done using Stata
14 software (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA) to identify the
predictors of successful VBAC using exposure variables such as
a history of VBAC, history of vaginal delivery, cervical dilatation,
membrane status and previous indications of CS. Forest plots
were used to show the prevalence of successful VBAC in Ethiopia.
Also, subgroup analyses were conducted using the regions and
publication year of the studies. Also, sensitivity analyses were
computed to assess the stability of pooled values to outliers.
The authors checked for potential publication bias using visual
inspection of a funnel plot and Egger’s regression test. Also, a
p-value <0.05 for I2 statistics was used to determine the presence of heterogeneity. The results of the review were reported
according to the PRISMA guidelines and presented using a narrative synthesis.

Results
Description of the studies
A total of 205 articles were found in electronic (205) and nonelectronic (15) databases. All articles were exported to the Endnote library and duplicates (75 articles) were removed. Also, a

total of 116 unrelated articles were excluded after titles and abstracts were reviewed. Then 28 articles were retrieved for detailed
examination. After a full-text review of those articles, 22 articles were excluded due to different populations and outcomes
of interest not being reported. Finally, full texts of the remaining
six articles and another six studies included in a previous study
were selected for the methodological quality assessment using
JBI critical appraisal tools (JBI, University of Adelaide, Adelaide,
SA, Australia). All appraised articles met the inclusion criteria and
were included in the final review (Figure 1).
Characteristics of included studies
Eight cross-sectional primary studies with a sample size of 2082
were used to determine the trend and pooled prevalence of VBAC
in Ethiopia. The prevalence of VBAC included in the reviews ranged
from 24.7 to 71.2%.9,10 Of those included studies, five were conducted in Oromia, three in Addis Ababa and the others were from
Amhara Region; Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples’ Region (SNNPR); and Harari Region (Table 1).
The trend and pooled prevalence of VBAC in Ethiopia
The rate of successful VBAC has increased in recent years in
Ethiopia from 24.21% to 38.15% (Figure 2). The overall pooled
prevalence of VBAC was 52% (95% confidence interval [CI] 40 to
65; I2=97.22%, p≤0.001 (Figure 3).
Predictors of VBAC
The association between successful VBAC and VBAC were examined based on the findings from eight studies. The pooled odds
ratio (OR) showed that women who had a history of prior successful VBAC were 4.16 times (adjusted OR [AOR] 4.16 [95% CI
2.65 to 6.53]) more likely to have a repeat successful VBAC than
those who had not had a prior VBAC. The association between
a history of vaginal delivery before CS and VBAC was examined
based on the findings from five studies. The pooled OR showed
that the odds of successful VBAC for women who had a history of

vaginal delivery before CS was 4.07 times (AOR 4.07 [95% CI 2.64
to 6.29]) higher than those who had no history of vaginal delivery
before CS. The association between cervical dilatation ≥4 cm at
admission and VBAC was examined based on the findings from
four studies. The pooled or showed that those women who had
cervical dilatation ≥4 cm at admission had 2.59 times (AOR 2.59
[95% CI 1.03 to 6.48]) higher likelihood of successful VBAC (Supplementary File 3).
Publication bias
The Egger regression test revealed no evidence of publication
bias among the included studies (p=0.512). In addition, a visual inspection of the funnel plot was done and is presented in
Figure 4.
Meta-regression to check heterogeneity
A meta-regression analysis was conducted since there was
statistically significant heterogeneity, with I2 test statistics
>0.05. The purpose of the analysis was to identify the source
of heterogeneity so that the correct interpretation of the findings is made. However, the meta-regression analysis found no

Subgroup analysis
Subgroup analysis was computed with the evidence of heterogeneity. Hence the Cochrane I2 statistic (97.22%, p<0.001)
showed the presence of marked heterogeneity in this study.
Therefore, subgroup analysis was implemented using the study

area (region) (Figure 5) and year of publication using random effects model analysis.
Regarding the year of publication, the prevalence of VBAC was
highest from 2021 onward (55% with 95% CI 34 to 75) and the
rate of VBAC was higher among studies conducted in Addis Ababa
(70% with 95% CI: 65 to 75) (Figure 6).
Sensitivity analysis
Sensitivity analysis was done by removing outliers and inliers and
no significant difference was seen. While removing outliers, we
noticed that the pooled prevalence of successful VBAC was 58%
(95% CI 42 to 74), and after removing inliers, the pooled prevalence was 46% (95% CI 28 to 64), so we can say this metaanalysis result is not sensitive.
Discussion
VBAC is crucial to deter operation-related maternal morbidity and
mortality. The success rate of VBAC was determined by obstetric characteristics such as successful vaginal delivery before CS
and successful history of VBAC. This systematic review and metaanalysis aimed to determine the trend, prevalence and predictors
of successful VBAC in Ethiopia.
376
International Health
Figure 6. Forest plot of the subgroup analysis based on publication year of successful VBAC in Ethiopia, 2023.
The pooled prevalence of VBAC in Ethiopia was 52%. This is
lower than the studies reported by Tahseen and Griffiths31 and
Rossi and D’Addario.32 This might be due to the difference in the
availability and quality of emergency obstetric care. Ethiopia still
needs to strive to achieve United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG-3) by ensuring the availability of quality obstetric care.
The rate of VBAC has increased over the last few years in
Ethiopia from 24.21% to 38.15%. This finding was supported by a
study done in the USA from 2016 to 2018 on recent trends in vaginal birth after CS.12 It indicates an improvement in the maternal
continuum of care and availability of emergency obstetric care
in Ethiopia.33,34 In contrast, this implies an increase in primary
and lower uterine segment CS.35 Moreover, it is vital to achieve

SDG-336 by decreasing maternal morbidity and mortality related
to repeated CS.
It was identified that prior successful VBAC delivery was significantly associated with current successful VBAC. This result is
supported by a number of studies and a systematic review and
meta-analysis.37–46 The possible explanation could be having a
prior VBAC might help the healthcare professional avoid making
an early decision on the mode of delivery because it suggests that
the primary cause of the CS is non-recurring. In addition, it might
indicate that a previous successful VBAC shortens the progress
of labour and decreases the likelihood of subsequent uterine
rupture and other morbidities.47 Furthermore, women who have
already successfully experienced a VBAC in the past may be psychologically well-prepared and aware of the benefits of vaginal
delivery.
It was identified that a history of previous vaginal delivery before CS was significantly associated with successful VBAC. This
finding is supported by studies in Nigeria,37,38 China,48,49 New
Zealand,42 Anatolia,43 New Delhi, India,45 Bahrain,47 Italy50 and
Thailand.51 This might be because those mothers who previously
encountered CS attributable to non-recurrent causes. Another
justification for this is that a previous vaginal delivery is linked
to shorter labour and a lower risk of uterine rupture.42 In addition, it might result in women feeling less worried about attending vaginal deliveries after experiencing a vaginal birth. Furthermore, women who have a history of vaginal delivery have better
knowledge of the advantages of vaginal delivery over CS, and the
likelihood of a failed trial of labour after CS increases with no history of vaginal birth.52
Those women who were admitted with cervical dilatation
≥4 cm were more likely to have successful VBAC. This finding
was in agreement with studies done in Nigeria,53 Anatolia,43
Bahrain,47 India,54 Italy50 and England.46 This might be in contrast
to the early initiation of labour, as cervical dilatation is now progressing at a faster pace toward complete dilatation.55,56 Another
possible explanation might be it is a result of the frequent occurrence of false labour, which may lead to intervention for dystocia
or prolonged labour.

Conclusions

This systematic review and meta-analysis revealed that a pooled
prevalence of successful VBAC is low in Ethiopia. However,the rate
of VBAC has increased over the last 3 decades. Prior successful
VBAC, history of previous vaginal delivery before CS and admission with cervical dilatation ≥4 cm were significantly associated
with successful VBAC. When counselling mothers with prior CS
scars, healthcare providers need to emphasize those factors significantly associated with a higher likelihood of successful VBAC
in Ethiopia to increase its prevalence.
Supplementary data
Supplementary data are available at International Health online.
